newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Crude Outlook - Weather leads way, grades off.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Crude Outlook - Weather leads way, grades off.

text.p: Crude oil price direction in the United States will be determined by the weather this week, and the effect cold temperatures will have on inventory levels for the start of the new year, oil traders and analysts said.
Weekly weather forecasts called for slightly lower temperatures in the key U.S. heating oil belt on the East Coast, and extended chills for much of the country.
Crude trading business was off to a slow start Monday due to Houston area ice storms, delaying commutes and knocking out power for thousands of Houston Lighting and Power Co customers.

Even though many crude players scoff at the lofty price for outright crude -- hovering around $26.20 per barrel for the spot February NYMEX contract -- there is no expectation the run higher will stop this week.
"I don't know if we'll get to $27.00, but there should be a run-up on Monday and Tuesday," said a Texas crude broker.
What happens after Tuesday depends mainly on the American Petroleum Institute (API) inventory statistics, the source said.
Bullish sentiment continued on the back of low distillate inventories, consistent demand and the cold.
"Short-term it's the cold, and longer-term there is the economy," said Bill O'Grady, senior analyst for A.G. Edwards & Sons in St. Louis, Mo.
O'Grady said the strength in the U.S. economy, with unemployment running at 5.3 percent and Gross Domestic Product around 3 percent, has buoyed oil products demand and outright crude prices.
"We've seen oil prices going up for almost a year, not any specific reason, but the underlying the whole move has been strong economic activity in the United States," O'Grady said.
He noted until the Federal Reserve tightens credit the market will be driven to remain at strong levels.
That strength, combined with demand in other regions, could be seen in the way the market shrugged at the re-entry of Iraqi crude flows, O'Grady said.

Since December 10, United Nations overseers have approved 26 oil contracts for the purchase Iraqi crude, effectively placing more than 555,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude onto world markets for at least the next six months.

Plentiful supplies of crude worked to deflate domestic grade differentials last week, notably in the key Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James market where premiums were sliced to only 10 cents over the spot West Texas Intermediate/Cushing.
Wide open arbitrage for bringing West African and Brent barrels to the U.S. Gulf spearheaded the price swoon, traders said, although demand has become more muted.

"I don't thing values will strengthen. West African barrels are being placed in the U.S. Gulf, Brent-WTI is widening and dated Brent is getting weaker, resulting in continued pressure on the grades," said a crude trader.
Physical Brent was dealt at February Brent minus 9 cents on Monday, a cent off the previous trade.
Late Friday, Brent was offered into the U.S. Gulf on a delivered basis for February 20-22 at March West Texas Intermediate minus 9 cents, and for Feb 18-20 at February WTI minus 73 cts.
Sour grades were also expected to track steady prices, though at the weaker levels established last week.
Slackening demand in the U.S. Gulf was also seen driving the competition for placing barrels, with large numbers of refineries scheduling turnaround programs starting in January.
((--New York Energy Desk, +1 212 859 1828))
